title: Potato price-fixing lawsuit alleging N.B. giants are part of 'good ol' boys network' goes ahead
summary: A lawsuit against major producers of frozen potato products, including two industry giants from New Brunswick, can go ahead, a U.S. judge has ruled.

image.caption: Cavendish Farms and McCain Foods, both with head offices in New Brunswick, are named in a U.S. lawsuit alleging price fixing in the frozen potato products market. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: New Brunswick
A lawsuit against major producers of frozen potato products, including two industry giants from New Brunswick, can go ahead, a U.S. judge has ruled.
Lawsuit alleges McCain, Cavendish and 2 U.S. companies conspired to raise prices
A lawsuit against major producers of frozen potato products, including two industry giants from New Brunswick, can go ahead, a U.S. judge ruled.
The class action lawsuit, launched two years ago, alleges antitrust violations by several manufacturers of frozen french fries, hash browns, tater tots and other potato products.

The four companies named in the suit — McCain Foods, Cavendish Farms, Lamb Weston and J.R. Simplot — make up a “good ol’ boys network," controlling the market in the U.S. and sharing information about pricing with each other, the suit alleges.
In a decision last month, Judge Jeffrey I. Cummings of the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois allowed most of the claims to continue.
Cavendish, which is owned by J.D Irving Ltd., has its head office in Dieppe and McCain has a head office in Florenceville-Bristol. Both Lamb Weston and J.R. Simplot are based in Idaho.
The lawsuit was filed in 2024 by Redner’s Markets, a Pennsylvania-based grocery chain.
It alleges that starting in January 2021, the four companies raised prices at “nearly identical rates around similar times” by sharing prices with each other on a program called PotatoTrack.

“Because the clients of PotatoTrack were limited to the four Producer Defendants and the United States Potato Board, the PotatoTrack reports allowed each Producer Defendant to assess critical data from the three other competitors,” the lawsuit said.

items: Alleged 'potato cartel' accused of conspiring to raise price of frozen fries, tater tots across U.S.

blocks.text: The defendants put forward a joint motion to dismiss the complaint, but Cummings mostly denied the motion.

The lawsuit said the four companies dominate the U.S. market for frozen potato products, controlling 98 per cent of it. The two Canadian companies, McCain and Cavendish, control 30 per cent and seven to eight per cent, respectively.

Any new competitors trying to enter the market would have a hard time even finding suppliers since the four major companies have long-established and exclusive relationships with potato growers, the lawsuit said.
The suit alleges that executives in the four companies develop close relationships through their membership in several potato organizations and their attendance at industry conferences.

The companies are also alleged to have knowledge about each other's business practices through co-packing arrangements in which on one manufacturer outsources part of its production to another company.
Cummings wrote that the companies didn’t make a good enough argument to have the lawsuit dismissed.
“It is well-settled that the exchange of price information among competitors is indicative of anticompetitive agreement,” Cummings wrote.
The four companies' control of most of the U.S. market is insufficient to prove a price-fixing agreement, but it makes it “more plausible” that it could happen, he said.
CBC News reached out to the four companies but did not receive a response from three of them on Thursday.
A spokesperson for J.R. Simplot said in an email that the company "is committed to competing fairly and with integrity in all markets where we operate and in compliance with applicable laws."

When the lawsuit was first brought in 2024, McCain said in a statement that it strongly disputed the allegations and would vigorously defend itself. The other three companies did not respond to requests for comment at that time.
